utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, before we hear the next witness, are there any other matters? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There are a couple of matters, Your Honour. The first matter I would seek to raise is this: That the current witness has provided -- we've been provided with some lengthy proofing notes from this witness. Now, they have -- we have not had the opportunity to put those to the accused man, Mr. Halilovic, as yet. What I thought would be the right course to take is to allow the witness to give his evidence in chief, first of all, and -- and then after that seek perhaps a short amount of extra time in order to acquaint Mr. Halilovic with what's in those notes, and it may be then that after the evidence in chief that will go quicker than if we have to go it in the abstract before we commence. It may be appropriate to take the break at that time in any event, and then we may not suffer any great delay. It is desirable, if all possible, for the Prosecutors to provide us with the proofing notes in a language the accused person understands because these -- these proofing notes sometimes contain more detail or advance or change the statements that were originally provided. And if we get them late, it can cause embarrassment. And it may be that on this occasion it won't, and I think we should press on, and I'm not asking for any adjournments right now, but I just mention that because it has the capacity to cause trouble. Maybe it won't in this case. So that's what I want to say about that particular proofing note issue. Your Honours, the next issue I wanted to raise was one concerning the following witness, Mr. Okic. We received from the Prosecutor by e-mail an indication that that particular person, last name Okic, wishes to speak to the Defence team. Now, we are prepared to speak to him, and we've made contact with the Victims -- VWS unit in order to bring that about. But they were unable to come back to us before court commenced today, and I think their indication was they were having trouble locating him. I don't know why that was, and it may not mean anything. In any event, we do wish to do that. And it may be that when the current witness, Mr. Tirak, is finished that Mr. Okic will have been found and then that will be an opportunity for the Defence to meet with him and see what it is that he wants to say to us, if anything, at that time. Now, we know -- we know no more than what I've told Your Honours at this point now, but we -- I thought it was best to raise it and prudent to raise it now, so I do. Therefore, when the current witness, Mr. Tirak, is finished, we may then seek -- depending on what we're told by the Victim and Witness Unit, we may seek a further short period of time to speak to him. Now, these matters are unfortunate. They're just matters that have arisen. And -- and I raise them so that the Court is informed of what the difficulties are. The third matter I wanted to raise is -- is one which might require some -- some argument at some point. I'm not sure if it will or it might. But it's the matter of Vehbija Karic. Now, that matter has got to be resolved and it should be resolved now, either today or tomorrow. Your Honour, Mr. Karic was interviewed and was the subject of a deposition before Ms. Featherstone, an officer of this court, some time ago. That was, as I understand it, videotaped, recorded, a transcript was made, and that evidence is admissible as evidence in chief. Now, on the occasion when that was done, Your Honours will -- will have to consider the content of that -- of that deposition because it really did feature some unusual features, and they'll be the subject of submissions in due course. But before we get to those submissions, the time has now come, really, for that deposition to be played to the Court because we've now had evidence from various witnesses, some of whom say that Mr. Karic did not say any of the outrageous things that are attributed to him, some of whom say that he did say those terrible things. And really now the time has come. We're nearly at the end of the Grabovica case. And whatever reasons there were for delaying in the past, have now evaporated. There's another reason why haste is needed. My instructions are that Mr. Karic is a person who has got -- has suffered for a long time with stomach cancer, and that's the reason why some time ago the procedure was adopted that the deposition be taken. And it should be recalled that he was called at that time to give the deposition and he was -- his evidence was led from him by no less than two members of prosecuting counsel, Mr. Withopf, and another Prosecutor, Ms. Tuma, both of whom were then on the team and neither of whom are now. Now, that evidence was led. Mr. Hodzic, who was then counsel -- no relation, I believe, to the current Mr. Hodzic who gave evidence here. Mr. Hodzic of counsel appeared and he expressed a view at the time that he was not ready to cross-examine and he was unable to cross-examine. He was asked by Ms. Featherstone to -- to reconsider that, bearing in mind the urgency of the situation and that there's a -- there's a discussion that takes place in the transcript about all of that. And he then did agree to -- to cross-examine, but he'd indicated a number of shortcomings that he suffered from, one of which was that he was seeking to be withdrawn from the case. Now, as a result of all of that, what I'm submitting is that there is a time pressure with Mr. Karic. It's a very important time pressure. The Defence wants to be able to cross-examine him further because, as you'll see when you see the transcript, and -- and watch the -- the tape, of course, you'll see that there was anything but a proper cross-examination conducted. And I make no -- no criticisms at this stage. Unfortunately, it will be my lot to make some criticisms later about that. But at this stage what can be said is that counsel very properly indicated that he just wasn't in a position to proceed properly. And in any event the Defence now wishes to further cross-examine Mr. Karic. And we don't want to do so with the shadow of illness or worse hanging over him anymore. Now, our understanding is that he is alive, in Sarajevo, and unwell, and that there is a time pressure about these things. So it's my submission now that the Prosecutor ought to interpose or build into the case, at this point now, seeing as it's come along, the deposition of Mr. Karic. An arrangement should be made to make him available for further cross-examination by the Defence, and in particular the Defence would indicate that we have no objection and indeed it looks likely that it would be the only possibility that that cross-examination took place by videolink because of the health situation. Now it's -- in the first instance it probably is up to the Prosecutors to indicate what his health position is. But our understanding is that he's unwell and it may be an issue for him to travel. He certainly was on the videolink during the course of the deposition that was taken. So that's matter I raise now. It was indicated by my learned friend Mr. Re in the past that the Prosecution was going to turn its mind to this question. In my submission, the moment has now arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I turn to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- about those three issues. One is about the proofing notes. The other is about Mr. Okic's testimony. The third one is Mr. Karic's deposition matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the three issues. The first one, the Prosecution doesn't object to the Defence seeking an adjournment to put the proofing notes to Mr. Halilovic. The second matter was their speaking to Mr. Okic. Yes, Mr. Okic did ask to speak to the Defence yesterday. And the Prosecution has tried to facilitate that through VWS. We understand that Mr. Okic will be brought here at some point this afternoon in case his evidence is reached. We certainly don't object to an adjournment for the Defence to speak to Mr. Okic before he's called. The third matter my learned friend Mr. Morrissey just raised on the matter of Mr. Karic. Mr. Morrissey seeks resolution of the matter either today or tomorrow. We have a witness awaiting, ready to give evidence. Could the matter await til tomorrow and the Prosecution will be in a proper position to argue the matter properly tomorrow, if it's suitable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, as for the first matter, I believe that the request from the Defence is granted. But as for the translation of the proofing notes into the B/C/S, I'm afraid that is not the usual practice of this Tribunal. Usually the proofing notes should be very short, very concise, and at this moment we don't see any Rules saying that the proofing notes should be translated into a language that the accused himself could understand. As for the second matter, we'll try to find a time for the Defence to meet Mr. Okic, since both parties agreed on this matter. But, however, this kind of practice should not be encouraged because we would like to hear his live testimony first. As for the third matter, well, since the Prosecution is not in the position to deal with it at this moment, so we might postpone it until tomorrow. I hope this matter could be done as early as possible since we are approaching to the end of the Prosecution's case very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And there are also several matters on my agenda. The first one is about the scheduling for tomorrow's hearing. I understand Mr. Morrissey will appear in an Initial Appearance. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't appear anywhere unless I'm -- I'm released by this court because my duty is to be at this court. But I've been asked to appear as duty counsel for the second time in the matter of Miletic. And if this Court is prepared to release me for a brief period of time, then that's what I'll do. But as I made clear to those who sought to engage me, my duties are in this court, so I do ask of the Court for the indulgence to release me for a period of time. I estimate that we won't need more than 15 minutes of court time because I've been told that the hear willing only take half an hour, and it's likely that if it coincides with our break, then a further 15 minutes should do it. And, Your Honours, I do seek that leave. Mr. Miletic is in a difficult position because he hasn't settled on counsel of his choice yet and it's probably in the interest of justice as somebody who has as slight familiarity of it as I do go to represent him. That might save more time than for the Tribunal, generally speaking, even though it costs 15 minutes here. But I make it quite clear that that's only on -- only if I'm released by this Chamber, because I'm appearing for Mr. Halilovic and that's where my first loyalty and connection lies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. So tomorrow afternoon we'll sit from 2.15 to 3.45. Then we'll take a break for an hour, and we'll restart our case at 4.45 until that Initial Appearance is over., whichever is later. Then we'll resume our hearing until 7.00. I hope 45 minutes will be enough for the Initial Appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, those instructing me are the Registry. They are in charge of -- of briefing duty counsel. And I'm told that that is likely, and the small contact I've had with the other Chamber indicates that that is likely as well. So should it appear that it's going to run over that time, I'll endeavour to withdraw from that obligation immediately. But that's what I'm told is the situation now. So I'm grateful to Your Honours for giving that indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. By the way, there's a matter that I have to mention at this stage, that is, we might have a break starting from 25th April for two weeks. So when the Prosecution's team is arranging for the testimony of the witnesses, they should take that break into consideration. Of course we are still waiting for the confirmation of any formal decisions concerning with other cases, but -- but anyway, I have to inform the parties beforehand, so everybody should be prepared for that two weeks' break. The third matter is a Defence motion on use and admission of the statement of the accused person obtained under coercion, filed on March 30th, 2005. The Trial Chamber received a list of the exhibits that the Prosecution intends to use during the testimony of the witness Zlatan Okic. This list was sent on the 29th March 2005. Witness Zlatan Okic is scheduled to appear before this Trial Chamber later this afternoon or tomorrow, the 31st of March, 2005. On the list there appears a document which is not indicated on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This document is a statement of Mr. Sefer Halilovic, given on the 12th November, 1993 to the State Security Service of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We only received these filings today, and I wonder, is there any response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I was told there is something wrong with the LiveNote. Well, I would like to hear from the Prosecution their response to this filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution's response to the filing of the Defence to exclude the records of -- or the statement to the Bosnian State Security. The Prosecution's response in general -- I wasn't prepared to answer it in full at this -- at this moment, but I can certainly respond in general terms as to what the Prosecution's response and the proposal for how the Trial Chamber should deal with this is. The Prosecution will be pressing for the admission into evidence of the statement of the 8th of November, 2003 to Bosnian State Security. I said "2003". I meant 1993. The Prosecution takes issue -- I won't go into it at the moment, there's too much detail there. I think we received this on Friday or Thursday afternoon, just before Easter, Easter break. The Prosecution takes issue with many of the matters raised in the Defence motion, many matters which the Prosecution says or submits assertions as opposed to matters which are properly the subject of putting into argument. For example, paragraph 5: "During the period of about three weeks Mr. Halilovic was confined to his house and then kept under de facto house arrest," which is footnoted to some evidence Mr. Hodzic gave last Thursday. The Prosecution submission in relation to that and many other assertions contained in the motion are that that's hearsay evidence which should not -- which should be properly tested on the application rather than footnoted to some small reference, perhaps not on point given during the evidence. That's just -- that's just one which I have referred to in passing. The Prosecution, of course, accepts that it bears the onus of establishing that a statement by the accused is -- is voluntary and should not be excluded under Rule 89(D) or Rule 95, and of course the Trial Chamber's guidelines on the admission -- admissibility of evidence refer to Rule 95. The Prosecution does not -- or submits that the references or the passage in that particular motion referring to Rule 42 do not apply to this particular interview because it was to Bosnian State Security in 1993, before the Tribunal even existed, and Rule 42 only -- and Rule 43 only apply to accused or suspects being interviewed by the Prosecution, which was of course established after the Tribunal was established, and those parts of the submission are irrelevant. The Prosecution has a witness here ready to give evidence who was present during the taking of the statement. Your Honours have seen the statement. It's been provided to the Trial Chamber and, of course, to the Defence, and proofing notes which I took yesterday when I interviewed the witness, which of his anticipated evidence further clarifying the circumstances of the taking of the statement. The Prosecution's submission is that this is a matter for -- for evidence. It's not a matter which should be decided on paper. It's a matter which should be decided by hearing from a witness who was actually present when the interview was taken, that is, Mr. Okic. From Mr. Okic's statement, he makes fairly strong statements that the interview was entirely voluntary and that Mr. Halilovic didn't ask for a lawyer and that Mr. Halilovic was treated with the utmost respect, was in uniform, had his weapon with him, was brought there every day by a military police officer, had breaks, and approved basically every sentence or every word in the statement before it was finished and before he signed it. Now, the Prosecution would argue that prima facie that gets it over the voluntary -- the hurdle of voluntariness, the Prosecution getting the Prosecution over the hurdle, which is of course the -- in our submission would shift it back to the Defence to an evidentiary onus to rebut, to rebut that. But having said that, the Prosecution submits that it is a matter in which the Trial Chamber should hear evidence as to whether or not the statement was voluntary or -- or coerced and was not oppressive. There is a possible procedure which as far as I'm aware -- or we are aware hasn't been used in the Tribunal before but was expressly approved in the Celebici Appeals decision at paragraph 542 and 543, which refers to the possibility of having a voir dire as to the admissibility of a confession or a statement as Your Honours are no doubt aware, it's a fairly common common-law procedure in which both parties give evidence on a particular point of the admissibility of evidence of a trial within a trial. And the Celebici Appeals Chamber expressly said that there was nothing -- that it would be: "A state of this procedure is not expressly provided for in the Rules; however, does this is does not mean that it would be unsuitable for a Trial Chamber to utilise it if a particular case -- if in a particular case it thought it appropriate." So there is express approval from the Appeals Chamber to utilise that procedure if the Trial Chamber thinks it's appropriate. So the Prosecution's submission, without going into too much detail, would -- line by line in response to the Defence motion at the moment is to hear the evidence of Mr. Okic as to the circumstances of the taking of the statement and then to rule after -- after cross-examination as to whether or not it is this -- the statements are admissible. Which brings me to the other point Your Honour has raised, and that is there is in fact a second statement which is very much germane to these proceedings, which was taken on the 12th of September -- sorry, 12th of November, 1993, again by Mr. Okic and Mr. Popovic. That particular statement is -- for a reason I -- I just cannot -- I don't know and I cannot explain, but I suspect was to have to do with it not being translated -- was not only the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list, but it's certainly a document that the Prosecution says having only -- only located it yesterday, when I was preparing or proofing Mr. Okic, is certainly highly relevant to the proceedings and was certainly disclosed - I think it was in September last year - to the Defence and we would submit there is no prejudice to the accused in putting that particular document into evidence, it being merely another statement taking -- taken during the course of the interviews the accused made to Bosnian State Security in November 1993. We'd submit it's certainly something which any prejudice could be cured by an adjournment, if necessary, to take instructions, but the Prosecution wouldn't think it would be the subject of too many instructions because it is -- the Defence challenge to the record of interview is as to whether it was coerced, whether it was taken in oppressive circumstances. So we'd be moving orally to amend our Rule 65 ter exhibit list to add that second document to -- to the list. If I could -- there is a reason -- if I could just find the document. The English translation, which is at page 8 of the document we circulated to Chamber -- to the Chamber's legal officer and the Defence yesterday, shows precisely how relevant that particular interview is to the proceedings. I'm sorry, it starts at page 7, where it says: "Sometime in early September 1993, I received an order from the commander of the Main Staff to make preparations for and execute Operation Mostar. I do not propose -- do not know who proposed this order. After receiving an order to carry out an inspection in the zone of responsibility, the 4th, 6th, and 3rd Corps and the authorisation to conduct combat operations in Operation Mostar, an operational plan was drawn up which was approved by the commander of the Main Staff ..." and so on. It then -- it then goes on to Mr. Halilovic saying that he wanted a force of at least 300 men, some who would be found in Sarajevo, the commander of the Main Staff - that's Mr. Delic - accepting the proposal. Mr. Halilovic presenting it to the commander of the 1st Corps, General Karavelic, Karavelic resisting it, saying that he needed the 300 men. Mr. Halilovic -- this is at page 8 -- saying in this -- he said: "I then issued an order to the 1st Corps commander. In this order we suggest that it would be a good idea to allocate troops from the 9th Motorised Brigade, the 10th Mountain Brigade, and Delta and we -- of course we took into account the opinion set out by the 1st Corps commander earlier, that he could not allocate troops from other units. In the conclusion of the order I wrote that I was assuming full responsibility for any potential repercussions which could ensue in Sarajevo." It then goes on to -- talking about the arrival of the men in the 9th and the 10th in Jablanica, Mr. Halilovic contacting Ramiz Delalic, Celo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we are not going into the details of that statement at this stage, and I believe that you made it very clear you want to amend the 65 ter list, to add this statement into your document list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct. I was merely using that to illustrate its relevance and, we say, importance -- albeit at a late stage, importance to the Prosecution case, it being a contemporaneous statement in November 1993 of the accused, a contemporaneous signed statement, as to his version of -- of what occurred. And in the Prosecution's submission, it is of the utmost importance that the Trial Chamber has the benefit of that particular document. That is, of course, subject to any ruling as -- ruling its admissibility into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we understand the position from the Defence from your filings, but I'll give you one minute to state it in a very concise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be less than one minute and not the repeat our submission. But there are a number of matters with which we take issue with the submission of the Prosecution. The first one is the suggestion that the evidence which has been referred to in our filing is hearsay evidence. Apart from the fact that hearsay evidence is admissible in this court, this evidence was in fact very direct evidence about the matters which are relevant to this filing, including the testimony of Mr. Kapur and Mr. Hodzic and also including the letter of Mr -- or sorry, the statement to the Defence of Mr. Popovic. Secondly, and as very properly pointed out by the Prosecution, the burden of establishing the noncoersive nation of the taking of that statement is upon the Prosecution and not upon the Defence. Thirdly, my colleague from the Prosecution suggested that Rule 42 would not apply to a statement taken by authorities other than the Office of the Prosecutor. And I direct the Trial Chamber to paragraph 29 of our submission -- of our filing, where we have referred to precedents which suggest the exact opposite in the Delalic and other cases. Finally, concerning this issue, the Prosecution has suggested that at the time the Tribunal didn't exist. Well, the Tribunal was established in May 1993 and the statements were taken in November of that month. Concerning the reasons why this statement was not put forward at an earlier stage or that the application for the amendment of the list was not made any earlier, the Prosecution has suggested that this may be a matter of translation. With respect, the Defence disagrees, since we have received translation of that document, I believe, in the autumn of 2003. We received the B/C/S version in September and the English translation shortly thereafter. Finally, concerning submissions, as for -- to the prejudice to the Defence of amending that list yet again, I think the burden is the other way round; that it is for the Prosecution to establish good cause and that they have failed to do so at this stage. But if more detailed submissions were to be made by the Prosecution at a later stage, we'd be -- we would be asking to be heard about our reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as the parties understand that we have two motions in front of us, one is concerning of the statement on the 8th November 1993 and the other is on the 12th November 1993. As the first submissions, I do not believe this Bench is in the position to make a ruling at this stage. We'll give more time to the parties, especially the Prosecution, to prepare their oral submissions when we come to the next witness. As for the second motion filed by the Prosecution, which is concerning with the statement of Mr. Halilovic on the 12th November 1993, this Bench believes the Prosecution is trying to introduce a new exhibit not included in its Rule 95 ter exhibit list at this stage of the proceedings. The Trial Chamber believes that this has not been done in compliance with the Rules because we do not want to see a pre-emptive attack from one party to another and caught the other party unprepared in these proceedings. The Prosecution has not shown good cause as to why this document should be added on its exhibit list at this stage. The Trial Chamber finds that the introduction and use of this document at this very advanced stage in the proceedings would be infringing upon the rights of the accused to a fair trial and his right to have adequate time to prepare his defence. Therefore, the Trial Chamber does not allow the introduction and the use of this statement during the testimony of witness Zlatan Okic. It is so decided. We'll find another time to discuss another statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something from Your Honours's ruling, and that relates to -- you said "we'll give more time to the parties to prepare their oral submissions when we come to the next witness." Is the Trial Chamber prepared -- proposing to hear the evidence of the witness and then take the oral submissions as to the admissibility of that document, having heard the witness's evidence as to how the statement was taken, or is the Trial Chamber proposing to adopt another course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on this matter, I believe that in the Defence filings they asked the Trial Chamber to forbid the use and the admission of that document, so before we hear the next witness, Mr. Okic, we have to decide -- we have to decide whether we should allow this document to be used or not. As for the admission of the document, we'll deal with it at a later stage. So maybe before the next witness, we'll hold a very short hearing like this one. Well, there's a very small matter which is kind of housekeeping, that is, concerning with Mr. Josarevic's documents. We believe that the Defence has objected to the admission of the Prosecution's document MFI204, 205, 210, 212, 218 on the basis that the witness had not seen those documents prior to proofing session with the Prosecution. The Defence submits that when a document has not been seen by the witness or where the security administration of the ABiH has not received it or had no reason to know about the document, the document should not be admitted into the evidence. The Trial Chamber recalls the guidelines on the admission of the evidence issued by the Trial Chamber under Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This Bench reminds the parties of the basic distinction that exists between the admissibility of documentary evidence and the weight of the documentary evidence that's given under the principle of free evaluation of evidence. The mere admission of a document into the evidence does not in itself signify that the statements contained will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. The practise is therefore in favour of admissibility of the Rule. This Bench finds that there's no blanket prohibition to the admission of documents simply on the grounds that a witness has not seen the document before proofing by either party. The Trial Chamber has assessed the relevance and the probative value of each document and has decided as follows: For the Prosecution's exhibit, document MFI 210 and 212 are admitted into the evidence. Document 204, 205, 218 are not admitted through that witness, but without prejudice to further application for admission. The Trial Chamber also noted that the Prosecution did not object to the admission of the documents tendered by the Defence. The Trial Chamber has assessed the relevance and the probative value of each document and has decided as follows: The document 219 -- yes, I think we have some technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The document 219, 220, 222, 224, 226, 227, 228, 229, 230, 231, 232, 233, 234, 237, 238, and 243 are admitted into the evidence. The documents 223, 236, 239, 240, 241, 242, and 244 are not admitted into the evidence through that witness without any prejudice to further applications of admission. The registrar has informed the Trial Chamber that the document 203 is identical to the exhibit D137. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will not admit this document into evidence. The Defence also tendered document 221. This document is essentially the same as Prosecution's document 215 with a different translation. This Bench would request the parties to discuss the matter of the translation of this document and to inform the Trial Chamber which of the documents they feel would be best admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. Yes, at this stage, could we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Sachdeva will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name, your place, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: My name is Tirak Dzevad. I was born on the 31st of October, 1938 in Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about your background and I will ask you leading questions in this regard. In 1975 you did your military service in Zadar and Krajovac [phoen] for 10 months and you were part of the anti-aircraft artillery unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the army in order to act in the defence -- anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had the rank of sergeant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, from 1976 to 1987, you were employed in the military factory called Famos, which made armoured vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes, between 1976 and 1987, I was at Famos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were given the rank of captain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes, since it was a military production plant, I had a contract on the basis of which I was formally made a captain, so that I -- that was because of the confidentiality of military information as to what was being manufactured there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. From 1987 to 1992, you worked at the private enterprise company called Aret in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From August or September 1992, you then joined the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the 1st Corps, which unit were you employed with?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Initially and until the end of 1992, I was in the 6th Mountain Brigade and I was an assistant commander for logistics. After that, in the beginning of 1993 and thereafter, I moved on to the logistics base of the 1st Corps in Pazaric, where I was the commander of this logistics base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just please tell the Court briefly the area of responsibility of the 6th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: At that time, when I was there, the area of competence of that brigade was the area around the -- Grbavica, Hrasno Brdo, and Hero's Square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your term with the logistics base in Pazaric, did you join the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes. After the 6th Corps was formed, I moved to the 6th Corps and I was the Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I think by the end of May or the beginning of June, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from your military deployments, did you always live or have you always lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I was in Sarajevo since 1963, but prior to that I was living in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you some questions about the 1st Corps and -- and we're going to deal with that right now. Firstly, when you were at the 1st Corps, who was the commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: At that stage, the commander was Mustafa Hajrulahovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Talijan. Yes, that was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you recall at that time, roughly how many brigades comprised the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you precisely --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness. It's not the witness's fault. I just would ask that it be clarified what time my friend is talking about when he asks that question. He refers to a -- "at about that time," and it ought to be specified what time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm referring to the time the witness was actually part of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were part of the 1st Corps, can you tell the Court, please, roughly how many brigades comprised the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think there were about 10 brigades in the city itself and two outside the city, plus a number of units within the framework of the Operational Group in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some names of the brigades that were within the city of Sarajevo, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I'll try. As far as I can remember, it was the 1st Brigade, then the 2nd Vitez Brigade, the 3rd Brigade, the Dobrinja Brigade. I can't remember what exactly the name of that brigade was. Then there was the 6th Mountain, where I was, the 101st. They merged afterwards. And then the 9th Mountain, the 10th Mountain Brigade. I can't remember -- I might have missed one or two. It's a bit difficult to remember after 12 years. Apart from that, there was the 4th Motorised Brigade at Hrasnica, then the Pazaric Brigade, and the Foca Brigade, and a number of units within the framework of the -- this operative group in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to concentrate on the 9th and 10th Brigades. What do you know about those two brigades, given your participation in the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Those two brigades were quite well known within the framework of the 1st Corps as brigades which, if I may say so, were prone to accidents. They caused incidents quite often, and sometimes they even mistreated the population and there had been any number of complaints about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "mistreated the population," could you please elaborate for the Court.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, I can quote one example. It could happen that people walking around town were simply stopped, picked up, and taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people military personnel or civilians?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I don't know, but generally speaking mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they picked up from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Most frequently in the old part of town, in the area called Ferhadija -- anyway, the old part of town, at least on the basis of what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you know, where were these trenches that therm taken to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yours, perhaps -- would the witness please excuse me for one moment, please. Your Honours, this evidence is being led in a very general way. Now, there's nothing against hearsay being led per se, but we need to know whether this witness is giving evidence from his own knowledge or whether it's from what he was told. And that should be made clear, in my submission, before this goes any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that evidence is from the witness's experience. And of course the Prosecution could be more specific on this aspect and the Defence has the opportunity to cross-examine on this issue. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question: From what you know, where were these trenches that people were taken to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Mostly in the direction of Trebevic, a hill above Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these trenches at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Of course. Trenches are always dug on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your military knowledge, was that area dangerous or safe?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: It was relatively safe, but any digging of trenches is risky for the simple reason that the enemy at the time would start shooting haphazardly, without any reason at all. You could never tell when they were going to start shooting. So that's why this digging of trenches was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any particular example of someone being taken to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I myself know of only one example. When my geography professor who at the time might have been 60 or something, and he complained that he was stopped on his way to the market looking for some food, and he was taken away to dig trenches. That's the only actual case that somebody complained directly to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, I can't recollect exactly when. I believe it was at some point in the fall of 1992. I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he did, who did he say told -- told him to go to the trenches or took him to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: At the time, the way he put it, it was Caco's men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Caco?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Caco was the commander of the brigade that was stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarity, what was the name of that brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I think it was the 9th Mountain. I seem to have confused all these names and numbers. But it was the brigade that was stationed in the area towards Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of somebody called Celo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I had never met him in person, but I do know that in much the same way as Caco's brigade -- basically these were the two units that caused most of those incidents in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your participation in the 1st Corps, how widespread was the knowledge of the reputation of these two brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, how could the witness possibly answer that question? It's a completely speculative question, calling for a speculative answer. It's not fair to the witness and not useful to the Court, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And you have to establish whether it's from his own knowledge or it's hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did soldiers in the 6th Mountain Brigade know of the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't object to this witness being asked the simple question: Did he know about the reputation? But this one, again, has just got that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- quality that's on the face of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The best way to elicit the evidence is to ask some question directly to this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of the reputation of these two brigades?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know of that reputation?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, especially in the course of 1993, whenever and for whatever reason I came to Sarajevo, the people I met very often complained of the fact that the members of those two brigades were causing trouble in Sarajevo, so to say I can say with a great deal of certainty that that was a widely held opinion in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these people that you met?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, normal people, my friends, professors, people who worked for the government that I worked with, soldiers, people from different walks of life, but they all lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said "soldiers" there.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that this was a widely held opinion in Sarajevo. On what basis do you say it was a widely held opinion in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Because I kept hearing about it from different people and therefore I can conclude that it was a widely held opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, at the time you were in the 1st Corps, who was the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told the Court about your professor and what he told you about being taken to the trenches. Apart from that, do you know of any other example of the [inaudible] the 9th and 10th Brigades in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness gave evidence that that professor was taken away by the 10th Brigade, by Caco's soldiers. Well, perhaps I should take that back and make it clear that he didn't mention either -- the 10th brigade at all. He simply said "Caco's soldiers." So to say now any other example of the 9th or 10th Brigade, well, the witness hasn't made it clear who did this outside of Caco's soldiers. And therefore, if he's got a specific example he wants to go to, it shouldn't be put in that -- in that way, merging the 9th and 10th Brigades, but it should be precise. Once again, there's a simple way to do it. A simple question would suffice. But merging those two has got that the problem I've pointed out in the past, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva, maybe you could clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about -- you've told us that you know who Celo was. Is there anything in particular that you could tell us about Celo's activity in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: As I've said, I myself did not have the opportunity to meet this man or to engage in any direct cooperation with him, but quite often I heard from many different people that, so to say, he was involved in things having to do with the exchanges of prisoners, cigarette smuggling, et cetera. I had heard it from others, but I've never myself witnessed any such dealings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of an area in Sarajevo called Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So to say, in the beginning of the war I myself lived in that part of town and an incident took place at that time as well. And members, so to say, of that Celo's group - the actual brigades had not been formed yet - they attacked the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Novo Sarajevo because the Territorial Defence people had argued with them for making trouble, and apparently they beat everybody up there. At the headquarters, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you hear of this incident?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: It was Mr. Fazlic who told me about it, Bahrudin Fazlic, who at the time was at the headquarters at the Municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Fazlic belong to the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes. Later he was the deputy commander of the 6th Corps. But in the summer in which that happened, in the summer of 1992, he was at the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of the Municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he tell you this incident took place in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, he told me -- I can't tell you with a great deal of precision, but maybe five or six days later, when we met, at the time when talks were being held about the setting-up of the 6th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that at the time you were in the 1st Corps Mr. Halilovic was the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you've also told the Court that your knowledge of the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigades was through meetings with soldiers, government people, and your friends. During those conversations you had, was there any indication about the involvement or - sorry, I withdraw that - the relationship between Mr. Halilovic and Celo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I don't know what specifically you mean by "relationship," but what was prevalent at the time was the perception that only Mr. Halilovic was in a position to somehow get them under control. But as to whether they had any sort of relationship, I suppose they did have a relationship along the lines of those they had with all the other brigades. I can't tell you. But most people used to say, "Okay, that's lucky, because Mr. Halilovic will be able to get them under control to a certain extent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate when you say "prevalent at the time." What do you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, at least on the basis of what I heard from other people, that the idea was that it was -- well, I suppose Mr. Halilovic will be able to tell you more precisely, but apparently many people complained to him. And as opposed to many others who did not even listen to these complaints, he was apparently in a position to exert some influence to a certain extent. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "people complained to him," which people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Mind you, I have no idea who specifically went to him to complain, but at the time people were talking and regardless of all the difficulties in the city at the time - no water, no electricity, no food - people always said that they felt unsafe, in a manner of speaking, in their own city, always referring to people from those two units. And as I say, quite frequently, I have no idea who explained to Mr. Halilovic. I'm sure that he can tell you, and I'm sure that complaints were frequent. But people would always end this debate by saying, "Well, it's a lucky thing that at least Mr. Halilovic can keep these people at bay to a certain extent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tirak, maybe my question wasn't clear enough, and I'm sorry about that, but when I -- when I asked you about a clarification of people, I mean whether they were military personnel or civilians, if you know that.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: The people who complained were usually civilians. I don't believe that any military men would have complained to Mr. Halilovic directly. They would have done it through their own superiors, or at least that's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to move to your role in the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's the right time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, I -- before the break, I told you we would talk about the 6th Corps, but I think I jumped ahead of myself there. So I want to just go back briefly to the units in the 9th and 10th Brigade, units of the 1st Corps, if I may. When you told us that the 9th and 10th Brigades had caused incidents and mistreated the population, who in the brigade did that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, one thing I know for sure is that this wasn't done by all the members of that unit. Many of the lads who were in that brigade did their job properly. Those were commanders, a specific group of people, I'm not sure how many. Some people around him, but not the entire unit. Those were the persons who did that. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Tirak, when you say "those were the persons who did that," what are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I think Caco, Celo, and a group of people around them. Mind you, not all the members of those units were the ones who caused trouble around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I know that because some people who were members of those units, let me say -- well, at least based on what I heard, did their job properly. They were brave lads who held their positions and defended the town but had no part in any of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any other brigades or units within the 1st Corps that had a similar reputation to the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Not nearly that kind of reputation as those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any other units within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had a similar reputation to the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Just excuse me one moment. Pardon me, witness. Your Honours, I'm not sure what the relevance of that question could possibly be. The witness is be -- is entitled to be asked about what he knows of the reputation, and we don't object to that. But this question just seems to be speculative and have a variety of faults, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are we going outside the scope of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, it's not outside the scope to have indictment, but I would prefer to make submissions about that in the absence of the witness, with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could try another way to see whether you could reach your goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, have you heard of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that looks like it's way outside of the indictment. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, does this have something to do with Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to explain this, if I may, in the absence of the witness. If that's not an inappropriate request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say that it is -- in my submission, I would say that it is relevant to the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigades -- the evidence of the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you insist. Witness, we are going to discuss some procedural matters, and Madam Usher will show you out of the room for a very few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been -- has participated in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for about one and a half to two years. Given that participation, the parameters of his knowledge are quite wide and it is entirely conceivable that he would know about other units within the army that had similar negative reputations, and I'm simply going to ask him about those units. And in his evidence -- in the anticipated evidence about those units, the inference, I would submit, would be that the 9th and 10th Brigades did indeed have a negative reputation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I fail to understand your logic of reasoning, Mr. Sachdeva, unless there's something specifically charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can see that there is nothing specifically charged about the Mujahedin in the indictment. In any case, I'll withdraw that. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we could recall our witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I apologise to you, and this kind of situation happened before. I hope you don't mind. Mr. Sachdeva, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Tirak. Mr. Tirak, relative to other brigades in the 1st Corps and within the army, how bad was the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to that. Your Honours, the witness has given evidence of what he knew about, and he indicated that he was in the 1st Corps. He's given -- he's already answered the question so far as he's able to, and he's given answers that were not objectionable and I didn't object. But now we're asking to expand this topic way out into, I think, within the army. Now, the witness has given evidence that he was in a logistics brigade for a period of time -- or a logistics unit at Pazaric. Before that, he was in the 6th Brigade. And after that, he joined the 6th Corps. Now, that's -- that's what he said. That's his evidence. And he's given his account of where these two brigades, so far as the rumours he heard, went, and in my submission, that's as far as it should go. My friend is really trying to open the same door a different way now, but in my submission, he just shouldn't be permitted to do it, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, I see no problem with this question. We'll see how far the Prosecution could go in this aspect. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, could you please answer that question. Or if you need me to repeat it, I will.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: My experience and my knowledge -- well, I can't say this about all the units of the BH army, because there were many units that I heard nothing about. They were far away. So I'm speaking about those that I know about and those that I'm familiar with. I believe that those two units had the worst reputation in terms of discipline, frequent incidents, that sort of trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will move to your role in the 6th Corps. When were you deployed to the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I was transferred to the 6th Corps when it was first set up. This was in late May or possibly early June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your functioning there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for completeness, who was the commander and the deputy commander of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: The commander was Mr. Salko Gusic and Mr. Bahrudin Fazlic was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the 6th Corps established?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: This was a time when hostilities started by the HVO and the 4th Corps was based in Mostar. The 4th Corps then fell apart, if I may put it that way. There was no real command. Units moved chaotically. It was virtually impossible to have any communication between the defence units in that area. It was then that the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the army Supreme Command, decided to establish the 6th Corps, using primarily some of the corps' units that were at that time in a state of chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give the Court some examples of these units that were in a state of chaos and were then brought under the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: At that point in time, there was a direct clash with the HVO units throughout the area. There had been more or less friendly relations with those HVO units up until that point, so many of the units were at a loss as to how they should react. Many of the communication lines had broken down and BH army units fled Konjic, for example, in a manner of speaking. Jablanica was surrounded. There was a state of chaos throughout the area, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which units came under your -- under the 6th Corps' control?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: The first order that we were given indicated that the following units should be resubordinated under the control of the 6th Corps: Units from Jablanica, from Konjic, from Visoko, from Gornji Vakuf, the Prozor Independent Battalion, as well as a company from the Hrasnica Brigade, and the Pazaric Brigade, as well as a number of smaller units. Soon after, however, the Prozoric and Hrasnica Brigades were returned to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unit from Jablanica, was that the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other units that operated within the 4th Corps that were eventually not brought under the 6th Corps' control?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: At the time, in the area covered by the 6th Corps, there were two units operating that were under the direct control of the Supreme Command Staff. I am talking about the Crni Labudovi, the Black Swans unit, and the unit under the command of Mr. Alispago, generally known as Zulfikar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were the Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps. Could you very briefly describe to the Trial Chamber your role, what you did in that function.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: When Mr. Gusic and Fazlic asked me to join their command, the basic reason was the fact that I had organisational skills. My military training was not that extensive, so that was not the chief reason. So the two of them ran the military aspect and I tried to get the units to know -- to get to know each other better. I set up a logistics base. In a manner of speaking, I was dealing with the less-military aspect. However, it was essential to set up an effective communications system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In trying to get the units to know each other, did you go and meet with any of the units of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes. It goes without saying. I visited all the units, seeing as I'd never been in the area before, it was also important for people to get to know each other so that they could work together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: This was in the summer of 1993. I can't be very specific about it. I think it was July. It was midsummer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to -- I will in the future ask you some detailed questioned about your meeting with the Prozor Independent Battalion, but for reasons of chronology, I will take you to another point in topic at this point in time. Do you know of a village called Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under whose control militarily was Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Formally, at least pursuant to the order that we had, it was under the control of the 4th Corps. The area covered by the 6th Corps ended at Jablanica, Donja Jablanica. Precisely for that reason, because it was clear that the 4th Corps was not able to keep that area under control at the time, the 6th Corps took over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time -- well, firstly let me ask you: When you say "at that time," roughly which time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I am talking about the first couple of months after the 6th Corps had been set up, until the situation normalised and the North Herzegovina Operations Group was set up that was to take control of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the 6th Corps took over control of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: The brigade that was based at Jablanica, the 44th Brigade. One thing you should know is that "control" does not imply that any of the units of the 44th Brigade were actually present there, because there were none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I will get to that later, but firstly, about Grabovica, do you know who was living in Grabovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: No, not specifically, but I know most of the people there were Croats. They said right away that they wanted no part of all that trouble. They just wanted to live on peacefully. But I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if these people who lived there were military people or civilians?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I have to underline this again: They said they wanted no part in that. In a formal sense, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, if you know, what was the atmosphere like in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I don't know what it was like at the time. I know there was a lot of tension between the ethnic groups. To the extent that we could, we tried to alleviate the tension, and that is precisely why the decision was taken to not have a BH army presence in Grabovica itself. But I must make this clear: I was not physically present there and I can't be more specific about the nature of the tensions that arose, if any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've said that there were no -- there was no military presence in Grabovica at that time. Do you know if that situation changed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I know that during the operation to lift the blockade of Mostar, BH army units came to the area and they hadn't been there up to that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know this, firstly?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I was informed by my deputy, Mr. Andric, and Mr. Fazlic when I came back from my assignment in Vakuf. That's when I returned to the 6th Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly when was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. It was sometime in September, but I'm afraid I can't be more specific about the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your information from Mr. Andric and Mr. Fazlic, what did you learn about this operation to lift the blockade of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that, Your Honour. Your Honours know that Mr. Fazlic was once upon a time a witness who the Prosecutor was going to call. Now they have renounced calling him by withdrawing him from the witness list, and this evidence is now a direct breach of the best-evidence rule because this witness now would be -- would be able to give an account of the conversation that he remembers, but he wasn't there and I don't think he's ever claimed that he was there, frankly. If I'm wrong about that. If he's going to be called to say that he was there and looking at these things, well, I've got no objection, of course. But as I understand the position, this witness is simply being called to say what he was told by Bahrudin Fazlic, who's also got the nickname of Braco, and that's a direct breach of the best-evidence rule. I'm not objecting on the hearsay evidence. That sometimes gets in and sometimes doesn't. But to renounce calling Mr. Fazlic and then to seek by the back door to lead in a conversation an account from him is just not permissible and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that objection went outside to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, it does because I know what's -- I know what is being sought to be -- to be led here, and the witness has had a conversation with Mr. Fazlic, and I object to that conversation being led because they're not calling Mr. Fazlic. This witness is just relaying that. So that's the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness is perfectly capable of giving evidence about his conversation with -- with another person. I see no -- I submit there's no reason why this evidence should not be admissible. As to the weight given to this evidence, that's another issue which is clearly stated in Your Honours' guidelines to this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear the evidence this witness is going to give, and we'll bear in mind this is hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I add one matter to that, please: The real issue here is not one of hearsay. I don't understand why my friend objects in that form. It's not a question of hearsay. It's a question of relevance. Now, the relevance of this witness's -- what this witness has been told is zero. Why the Prosecution is leading this evidence is to get before you what Mr. Braco Fazlic had to say. That's why it's being led. If my friend says I'm wrong about that, he can say so. But that really is why they're leading this evidence. If that's the case, then it's irrelevant for this witness to say what he said and what he did and so on, so it's -- so I just want it to be clear that's what the objection was. Now, if -- but I take Your Honour to have ruled on the matter of -- of my previous objection, so I just -- as long as that's clear that that's what my objection is, it's not -- it's not an attack on this witness at all but it's just the relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We understand that. And we'll take your objections into the consideration at a later stage. You may proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take this step by step. You said you spoke to Mr. Andric. What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: He said that the operation for the lifting of the blockade of Mostar was underway, but he said that he couldn't reveal too many details because not all communication went through the liaison centre at Konjic, the headquarters of the 6th Corps. That would have been the normal procedure. But that it went through the liaison centre at Jablanica. And he said that there was a command department of the -- of the forward command post that was leading that information. I was rather surprised by that because within the 6th Corps there were no plans for any such operation and because of that, I -- well, since the commander was absent, I went to see his deputy, Mr. Fazlic, to find out what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you ask Mr. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Well, I asked him to, so to say, explain to me in somewhat greater detail than Mr. Andric could have done what was actually going on and how come I myself, as the Chief of Staff, knew nothing about it, about this sort of operation. Then -- well, I'm going to try and kind of interpret everything that he said, but you have to take account of the fact that 12 years have gone by, I had not taken any notes or anything, so I can only tell you what I remember. So he informed me that a couple of days earlier they called him and Commander Gusic to Jablanica, and there were some members of the Supreme Command there, and Mr. Sefer Halilovic as well. And they were informed that the operation for the lifting of the blockade of Mostar would start and that in that operation, that there would be units from Sarajevo, Mr. Zuka's units, and they asked for three units from the 6th Corps to participate in that operation. They would have been the brigade from Jablanica, the 44th Brigade, and a unit from a brigade from Buturovic Polje, that is to say, the 45th Brigade, and the Independent Battalion Prozor. On that occasion, a more detailed explanation was given of the entire operation, and afterwards, on the day after, he was asked to issue relevant orders to those three units, which he did. And then I asked several questions. First of all, it wasn't quite clear to me because at that time we did not have sufficient provision, sufficient ammunition, or any other technical or materiel support for such an operation, and therefore it was not clear to me in what way such an operation would be conducted. And he was rather resigned in reply, and he said to me that it wasn't very clear to him either what was going on. And when I asked him what units those were, what units from Sarajevo had arrived to participate in that operation, and when he told me that it was the 9th and the 10th Mountain Brigades, I must say that I was rather surprised that it was precisely those units which had a very bad reputation that had been sent down there, instead of units which were much more capable and had a better track record in terms of being able to carry out such an operation. Thereupon, Mr. Fazlic told me that he had just found out that some crimes had already happened at Grabovica but at that stage he was not familiar with any details. And then he order me, in spite of the fact that I had only just arrived and I was quite tired, he ordered me to go back to Visoko and look for Mr. Delic, who was appointed commander of the BH armed forces and to report to him and to insist that those Sarajevo units should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please remove his hand from in front of his mouth, because we can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, sorry to interrupt you. You've just been asked by the interpreters to remove your hand so they can -- so the Court can hear your evidence properly, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, may I just stop you there for the moment, and I will allow you to continue in a minute. But I want to ask you: When you spoke to Mr. Fazlic, did he tell you who was to be the commander of this operation to lift the blockade of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: He then told me in so many words that Mr. Sefer Halilovic was in command of that operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you which other persons were involved in this operation to lift the blockade of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood the question. What people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, which other persons were with Mr. Halilovic in Jablanica at the time they met with Mr. Gusic and Mr. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK
utterances.text: He mentioned a number of names. I can't recollect all of them. If my -- if I remember properly, Karic, Suljevic, but I must say that I can't remember precisely, because -- but he did tell me precisely, but 12 years later it is a bit difficult for me to remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
